name: CAMEROON

flag.title: Tricolour & Star
flag.note: Green, red, yellow with gold star

lead: Cameroon sits at Africa's crossroads — thick rainforest meets open savanna, a volcano rises straight from the sea, and 280 languages fill the air. Geographers nicknamed it "Africa in miniature" because its landscapes pack in nearly every terrain the continent has: desert, jungle, highland, and coast, all within one country.
geo: Cameroon is shaped like an upside-down triangle. The south is dense equatorial rainforest; the centre rises to cool highlands; the north flattens into Sahel grassland near Lake Chad. The Adamawa Plateau runs like a green spine through the middle.

The coast faces the Gulf of Guinea, where Mount Cameroon — an active volcano — rises straight from the sea. The remote Dja Forest is one of Africa's best-preserved rainforest reserves, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
animals: Cameroon's rainforests shelter western lowland gorillas, forest elephants, and chimpanzees. The Dja Reserve alone hosts 100+ mammal species. Drills — big, brightly faced monkeys — live only here and on nearby Bioko Island.

Birdwatchers seek the Cameroon Highlands for 20+ birds found nowhere else on Earth, including the Bannerman's turaco with brilliant red wings. Leatherback sea turtles nest quietly on Atlantic beaches each year.
culture: Cameroon has over 280 ethnic groups — Bamileke, Fulani, Beti, Bassa and dozens more. The Bamileke are famed for elephant-mask dances where huge carved headdresses sway to thundering drums at royal festivals.
Food centres on ndólé (bitter-leaf stew with groundnuts), eru, and plantain pounded into fufu. Football is a national obsession — the Indomitable Lions won the Africa Cup of Nations five times.
history: Bantu-speaking peoples settled Cameroon's forests thousands of years ago. Portuguese sailors arrived in 1472 and named the Wouri River 'Rio dos Camarões' (River of Prawns) — giving the country its name. Germany colonised the region in 1884.

After WWI, Britain and France split the territory. French Cameroun gained independence on 1 January 1960. The British section voted to join in 1961, creating today's bilingual republic with Yaoundé as capital.
wows: Mount Cameroon is the tallest peak in West-Central Africa and one of the continent's most active volcanoes.
Cameroon has 280+ distinct languages — one of the highest concentrations per km² on Earth.
Debundscha on the Cameroon coast averages 10,000 mm of rain a year — among the world's wettest spots.
The Indomitable Lions were the first African team to reach a World Cup quarter-final, in Italy 1990.
Cameroon plays two national anthems at official events — one in French, one in English.
Lake Nyos released a deadly CO₂ cloud in 1986 in one of history's rarest disasters: a limnic eruption.
The Ngondo festival sends a diver into the Wouri River to deliver messages to river spirits — centuries old.

myths.fact: Cameroon holds every African terrain: jungle, savanna, highland, semi-desert, volcanic coast, and the wettest coastal spot on the continent.

myths.myth: Its two official languages cause constant tension
myths.fact: Cameroon is proudly bilingual — both languages appear on banknotes and signs, and Cameroonian Pidgin bridges communities daily.
